Astara Intelligence · Research

Automotive & Mobility
Investment Report

Q1 2026

Fewer deals, larger bets: autonomy, electrification and strategic capital reshape mobility investment.

Section 1

Executive summary

Q1 2026 recorded 97 investment entries in automotive and mobility, of which 91 include disclosed amounts. Total disclosed investment reached $26.93bn, with a median disclosed entry of $42.0m. At face value this places Q1 2026 close to the strongest Q1 periods in the dataset (2022–2026), but the quarter should be read as a concentrated market rather than a broad-based funding rebound.

The single largest entry, Waymo at $16.00bn, represents 59.4% of disclosed Q1 2026 volume, with the top 10 entries accounting for 81.4%. Capital is flowing into fewer, larger strategic bets — particularly in autonomy, electrification, robotics and shared mobility.

This accelerates a multi-year decline in total deal volume tracked since 2022: 609 (2022), 253 (2023), 272 (2024), 156 (2025), 97 (2026) — an 84.1% contraction in deal volume since 2022, compounding at a CAGR of −36.8%.

Advanced Mobility is the dominant vertical, with $22.24bn across 46 entries. The strongest subvertical is Autonomous, driven by Waymo, Wayve and Bedrock Robotics. The sector is no longer funding every mobility model equally: capital favors control points in the future mobility stack — autonomous driving software, EV platforms, battery value chains, charging infrastructure, robotics, telematics and data-enabled services.

Section 2

Q1 2026 market snapshot

Q1 2026 shows a high disclosed investment volume of $26.93bn across 97 entries. The average disclosed entry is $295.9m, but the median is much lower at $42.0m, confirming a skewed distribution shaped by very large transactions.

Section 4

Sector allocation

Sector allocation confirms that Q1 2026 is primarily an Advanced Mobility quarter ($22.24bn, 82.6% share). The second layer — Deeptech & Enabling Technologies, Shared Mobility, Mobility Intelligence and Ownership — represents different parts of the mobility value chain.

Figure 4 · Investment by vertical

Autonomous is the largest subvertical, with $18.39bn — reflecting autonomy megadeals and software-defined driving as a strategic control point. New Vehicles and New Energies form the next layer, linking vehicle platforms, batteries, charging and energy infrastructure.

Figure 5 · Top subverticals by disclosed investment
Section 5

Key investment themes

Autonomy becomes a capital-intensive strategic layer

Waymo, Wayve and Bedrock Robotics make autonomy the defining theme of Q1 2026. Investors are concentrating capital around companies that control autonomous driving software, AI models, vehicle operation systems or non-passenger autonomy applications.

Electrification moves beyond vehicles into infrastructure and materials

Rivian, Polestar, Redwood Materials and Fastned show electrification is not only about vehicle launches. The value chain includes battery materials, circular supply chains, charging networks and balance-sheet support for EV companies.

Robotics become an important category of the mobility map

Apptronik and Mind Robotics show robotics should be treated as adjacent to mobility, manufacturing and automation. The report keeps Deeptech & Enabling Technologies visible rather than hiding it as a miscellaneous category.

Shared mobility is more selective

Shared Mobility still attracts meaningful capital through Rapido and Zipline, but the pattern is narrower than earlier years. Capital favors platforms with scale, logistics relevance or clear geographic growth.

Data, telematics and intelligence remain strategic

Mobility Intelligence is smaller by disclosed amount, but Cambridge Mobile Telematics shows why it matters: connected data, driver behavior, insurance intelligence and fleet management can become high-margin layers of the stack.

Ownership and retail tech remain relevant but secondary

Kavak and other ownership entries show digital retail, used-car platforms and financing remain part of the landscape, though not the dominant story of Q1 2026 versus autonomy and electrification.

Section 6

Geography of Q1 2026 investment

North America accounts for $21.25bn in disclosed Q1 2026 investment, heavily influenced by Waymo. Even excluding Waymo, North America remains a leading region, but the gap with Europe narrows materially. The United States leads by amount, with the United Kingdom (Wayve, Zipline), Sweden (Polestar), India (Rapido), China and the Netherlands also material.

Section 8

Strategic implications

For OEMs

Autonomy, software-defined vehicle capabilities, EV platforms and strategic partnerships matter. Monitor not only direct vehicle competitors but autonomy providers, battery-material players and charging networks.

For distributors and retailers

Ownership and retail tech remain relevant for vehicle access, used-car platforms, financing and aftersales. Watch how digital ownership models interact with EV adoption and fleet channels.

For fleet operators

Telematics, predictive analytics and mobility intelligence are directly relevant to operational efficiency, insurance, maintenance, utilization and residual-value management.

For energy and charging players

Continued investment in charging and battery value chains. The opportunity is broader than stations: energy management, recycling, fast-charging networks, grid integration and fleet electrification.

For investors

Q1 2026 favors selective conviction over broad mobility exposure. Capital-intensive areas require patience, technical due diligence and an understanding of strategic buyers, public support and platform economics.

For public-sector and industrial strategy teams

Autonomy, robotics, batteries and charging infrastructure increasingly tie to industrial capacity, with implications for investment attraction, talent, land use, energy planning and advanced manufacturing policy.

Section 9

Early Q2 2026 watchlist

April 2026 includes 33 entries, 31 with disclosed amounts. Disclosed April volume reaches $4.43bn, median $30.0m. This is a watchlist only and should not be added to the Q1 core figures. It suggests continuity in Advanced Mobility — vehicle platforms, aviation, battery supply chains and advanced propulsion remain active.

Data limitations

The dataset is an investment-entry database, not a complete global market-sizing source. Entries are tracked from the web, saved and categorized. Some companies appear more than once because they received multiple entries in the period. Investor names are not always disclosed or meaningful; non-meaningful values were classified as Undisclosed.
